newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Planes bomb Afghan capital, Taleban attack in nort.
newsitem.headline: Planes bomb Afghan capital, Taleban attack in nort.

text.p: At least one opposition warplane bombed eastern Kabul, but residents in the Taleban-held Afghan capital said on Tuesday there was no apparent damage.
It was not immediately clear how many planes were involved in the raid at about 9:30 p.m. (1700 GMT) on Monday night, nor how many bombs were dropped.
The evening sky lit up as the purist Islamic Taleban militia fired anti-aircraft guns and even Kalashnikov assault rifles skywards in a noisy barrage.
Opposition planes bombed the Kabul airport area in the east of the city the previous two nights, killing at least six people and destroying three houses, witnesses said.
This week's air raids, apparently directed at the airport, which is used for military and civilian purposes, were the first since January, when eight civilians were killed and 52 wounded.
The Taleban, who captured Kabul in September, have been forced on to the defensive in the past few weeks after suffering humiliating defeats in opposition-held northern Afghanistan.
But Taleban officials said on Tuesday their forces based in the northern town of Baghlan had launched an overnight offensive towards the city of Kunduz, 65 km (40 miles) further north.

Taleban officials, quoted by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP), said their fighters had captured the town of Aliabad, 40 km (25 miles) north of Baghlan, on Tuesday morning and had gone on to seize Kunduz airport.
The officials said fighting was now going on near the city of Kunduz, which is held by various opposition factions, mostly loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
There was no independent account of the reported offensive.
"Some local commanders invited us to come to Kunduz," a Kandahar-based Taleban official, Wakil Ahmad, told AIP.
The Taleban force, estimated at about 3,000 strong, arrived in Baghlan last week after opposition forces drove it from the town of Pul-i-Khumri, 30 km (19 miles) south of Baghlan.

Opposition spokesmen had said earlier that Bashir Baghlani, a commander of the Hezb-i-Islami faction in control of Baghlan, had agreed to disarm and hand over the Taleban force to the opposition forces which captured Pul-i-Khumri.
However, a Western military source in Islamabad said it was clear that this had not happened. "There is hard evidence that Baghlani did not disarm the Taleban," he said.
